An explanation of how business needs get translated into requirements and different sub-types.

Business Needs

Business needs can include a description of capability needs (statements about what the organization wants to be able to do) or improvement needs (statements about what capabilities the organization wants to modify, remove, or decomission , i.e. increase efficiency, decrease costs, improve value).

Example: “We must unify our customer experience across our web site and our stores.”

Business needs may also surface as result of changes in the macro-environment (political, economic, societal, technological) or as a result of changes within the organization, i.e. changes in business strategy, business model(s), operating model(s), and enterprise architecture.

Solution Requirements

Solution requirements capture the overall characteristics of a business solution. It typically contains higher-level descriptions of the business capability needed. Solution requirements are eventually decomposed into business requirements and system requirement types (functional and non-functional). Additionally, they may encompass or touch upon some or all of the Operating Model dimensions:

  1. Governance
  2. Process & Function
  3. Performance Management
  4. Organization
  5. Knowledge and Data
  6. People
  7. Technology Enablement

Example: “The solution must integrate our sales process across our physical and digital retail channels.”

Business Requirements

Business requirements describe the changes needed by the business for the solution. They may be defined for six dimensions of the Operating Model, depending on the nature and scope of the solution and business vision:

  1. Governance
  2. Process & Function
  3. Performance Management
  4. Organization
  5. Knowledge and Data
  6. People

The last dimension of the Operating Model, Technology Enablement, is covered by the System Requirement work product.

Example: “A customer must be able to purchase from either our on-line or retail outlet, and pickup or return an item through either channel.”

As business requirements are analyzed and refined, additional details may emerge that will have an influence on other business requirements and system requirements, and vice versa. As a matter of fact, it's a common myth that business requirements decompose into system requirements, when in reality systems are just one way to meet business requirements, i.e. the other six Operating Model dimensions.

Some business requirements may be transitional, meaning they are one-time or short-lived requirements needed to transition to the future state. Some examples include: new branding, product merchandising display requirements, new/modified facilities, sites, physical plant and equipment, labor agreement changes, policy changes, or permits and license agreements. In practice, they could be flagged as transitional in a requirements register.

System Requirements

System requirements describe characteristics of a system or product that provides the technology enablement of a business solution. It describes how the product must function. They are typically categorized into functional and non-functional requirements.

A system requirements is a "statement that identifies system, product, or process characteristic(s) or constraint(s), which is unambiguous, clear, unique, consistent, stand-alone (not grouped), and verifiable, and is deemed necessary for stakeholder acceptability." (INCOSE 2010).

Example: “The system shall enable store associates to see a consolidated view of a customers’ POS purchases and web order history.”

Similar to business requirements, as system requirements are analyzed and refined, they may require certain business requirements to be revisited. Additionally, some system requirements may also be transitional, for example, data conversion from existing systems, or end user training. In practice, they could be flagged as transitional in a requirements register.

Functional Requirements

Functional requirements specify what the system or product must do. They describe the desired behavior and information that the solution will manage in a way that is independent of the technology that will be used to implement the requirement. This approach allows the logical essence of the requirement to be abstracted in a way that enables alternate technical implementation options to be evaluated later during design without technological bias obfuscating or substituting for the real requirement.[1]

Functional requirements are typically supported by shall statements, use cases, and user stories to provide further contextual descriptions about the system.

Non-Functional Requirements

Non-functional requirements are descriptions of the properties or characteristics that a system must exhibit or a constraint that it must respect; they are the qualities the system or product must have, or how well it does things

Decomposing Solution Requirements into Business Requirements and System Requirements


Many people confuse the terms business requirements and system requirements, and often believe they are the same. They are actually quite different. Business requirements define what must be delivered to provide value. System requirements describe what the proposed system will provide, in line with business requirements. According to Robin Goldsmith in his book Discovering REAL Business Requirements for Software Project Success, defining business requirements is the most important, yet least well performed part of system development. In fact, many organizations simply define system requirements and never define business requirements.

Business requirement are written in business language to describe what must be delivered to meet business needs. When delivered, business requirements provide value by meeting business objectives. In contrast, when most people use the term “requirements” they actually refer to the “hows,” albeit at a high level of abstraction and often subconsciously. There are many different ways or options to satisfy the business requirements. System requirements describe the high level design for a solution that is one of the possible ways to deliver the business requirements. The solution can work as designed, but will provide real value only if meets specified business requirements.

Problematically, many business analysts do not understand the difference between business and system requirements. In fact, many requirement books do not even describe business requirements, and almost always state that they are addressing requirements of a product, system, or software. Some sources even state that the difference between business and product requirements is simply the level of detail, which is sometimes referred as the “level of abstraction.” According to the same sources, business requirements are high-level and vague and decompose into product requirements, which are detailed. In their minds, if a requirement is detailed, it’s a product requirement; whereas if it is high-level and vague, it’s a business requirement. This is simply wrong.

The IIBA’s Body of Knowledge recognizes the difference between business and product requirements. However, most requirements tools vendors do not recognize the difference and focus entirely on defining functional and nonfunctional requirements. Functional and nonfunctional requirements are product requirements, not business requirements. Failing to recognize the difference between business and product requirements and failure to identify and define business requirements usually results in significant scope creep and in delivery of solutions that provide little business value.

According to research by the Standish Group, 45% of system functionality developed is never used. This is mostly a result of organizations’ failure to define business requirements. In addition, the vast majority of systems delivered fail to provide expected business value. This is evidenced by the quotes below.

  • 78% of Information Systems projects failed to realize even 50% of the originally identified benefits.” Source: Management Today
  • “Only 40% of CFOs find that their IT investments are producing the returns they expected.” Source: Gartner, How to Optimize IT Investment Decisions
  • “30-40% of systems to support business change deliver no benefit whatsoever.” Source: OGC, Successful Delivery Toolkit

The primary reason solutions provide little or no business value is because the underlying business requirements were not adequately defined, which is due to people believing that product requirements are the same as business requirements. So long as BAs and others continue to follow this flawed approach, they will keep generating the same poor results and they will keep fixing the wrong things, delivering functionality that is not used, and delivering solutions that provide minimal business value.

[1]. Adapted from:

  1. A Guide to the Business Analysis Body of Knowledge, BABOK Guide, Version 2.0.
  2. Mastering the Requirements Process, Suzanne Robertson and James Robertson, Addison
